text: and miconazole are all used topically. Topical antifungals are not well absorbed and infections extending into the eye require subconjunc- tival, intra-ocular, or systemic therapy. Systemic treatment may also be indicated when there is a poor response to top- ical agents, for fungal endophthalmitis, or for ocular man- ifestations of disseminated fungal disease. When systemic treatment is indicated intravenous amphotericin B is usu- ally given. Azoles may be given for less severe infections or as adjunctive therapy in severe infections. Oral flucona- zole and ketoconazole have better penetration into the cor- nea, aqueous humour, and vitreous humour than itracona- zole. Intravitreal injections may be required in infections unresponsive to systemic antifungals.3,4 Surgical debride- ment or excision may be necessary if the infection progresses despite appropriate antifungal therapy.1,2 1. Histoplasmosis Histoplasmosis is a systemic infection caused by Histo- plasma capsulatum, a fungus found in the soil in endemic areas, particularly at sites with heavy accumulations of bird or bat excrement. Infection is by inhalation of spores. Two types of histoplasmosis occur: • American histoplasmosis, due to infection with H. cap- sulatum var. capsulatum • African histoplasmosis, due to infection with H. capsu- latum var. duboisii H. capsulatum var. capsulatum is endemic in the central USA where 50 to 90% of the population is infected. Mild infections are generally asymptomatic. However, acute pulmonary infection can occur. Massive infection can be fatal. Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis can result in lung fibrosis and cavitation. Acute or chronic disseminated in- fection involving widespread infiltration of the reticuloen- dothelial system, is mainly seen in immunodeficient or im- munocompromised patients. Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii is found in Africa and may cause a chronic disseminated form of histoplas- mosis with focal lesions predominantly in skin and bone.
